274.title: The saint-soldier
274.hook: the Khalsa ideal holds prayer and courage together in one person
274.tomorrow: Two flags at the Akal Takht
274.howItsDone: Sikhs describe the Khalsa ideal as sant sipahi, saint-soldier: an initiated Sikh keeps the daily prayers and discipline and also stands ready to defend the weak and resist injustice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Rehat Maryada: a shared code. That closed the days on the Sikh way of life. Today a new stretch begins: sword and saint.

At dawn, someone sits cross-legged, eyes closed, lips moving with a prayer. Later that day, someone stands between a bully and the kid being bullied, and doesn't step aside. It's easy to file them in different drawers: the quiet one and the brave one, the monk and the firefighter. The Sikh tradition keeps asking a stubborn question: why not the same person, someone who prays at dawn and, when it's needed, stands in the doorway? Today: the saint-soldier.
screen: `ONE PRAYS AT DAWN.` → `ONE STANDS IN THE DOORWAY.` → `WHY NOT THE SAME PERSON?`

segments.voice: Sant is a saint, a holy person whose mind rests in God. Sipahi is a soldier, a Persian word; the English sepoy comes from it. Together, sant sipahi is a phrase Sikhs often use for the Khalsa ideal. It has a history. The first Gurus were teachers of the Name, poets and farmers. Then, in 1606, the fifth Guru, Guru Arjan, was executed in Lahore by the Mughal authorities. His son, Guru Hargobind, became the sixth Guru as a boy, and tradition says he put on two swords. One he called miri, worldly responsibility. The other, piri, spiritual authority. Both at once. Nearly a century later, Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa in 1699 and gave the idea its fullest form: keep the daily prayers and the discipline of the Name, and stand ready to protect the weak and resist injustice. Notice the order. The saint comes first, in the phrase and in the life. The daily prayers aren't a warm-up before the real work; they're the root, and courage grows out of them. Without the saint, the soldier is only force. Without the soldier, the saint may watch injustice and do nothing. Sikhs don't read this as a call to go looking for fights. A saint-soldier may never touch a weapon beyond the small kirpan. Their courage looks like telling the truth in a meeting, or refusing to laugh along. The prayer steadies them. The courage makes it real.
screen: `SANT — SAINT. SIPAHI — SOLDIER.` · `1606: TWO SWORDS, MIRI AND PIRI.` · `1699: THE KHALSA HOLDS BOTH.` · `THE SAINT COMES FIRST.` · then, large: `SAINT AND SOLDIER.`

segments.voice: First the saint: settle, and if you pray, use a line you know; if not, rest your mind on something good and true for a few breaths. Then the soldier: from that steady place, bring to mind one small brave thing waiting for you, a hard conversation, a truth to tell, someone to stand beside. Don't do it yet; just decide you will.
Sant sipahi. The saint-soldier: prayer and courage held together in one person, with the saint first.
Your line: saint and soldier. The prayer is the root; the courage grows from it. That's day two hundred seventy-four.

275.title: Two flags at the Akal Takht
275.hook: two Nishan Sahibs stand there, for worldly and spiritual sovereignty, the spiritual one slightly higher
275.howItsDone: Every gurdwara flies a Nishan Sahib, a saffron flag bearing the khanda; at the Akal Takht in Amritsar two stand side by side for miri and piri, and Sikhs bow toward the Akal Takht as the highest seat of Sikh authority.

segments.voice: Yesterday, saint and soldier, and Guru Hargobind's two swords. Today, those two swords become two flags.

Drive through almost any town with Sikhs in it, from Punjab to Surrey to Yuba City, and look up. Above the rooftops there's a tall pole wrapped in saffron cloth, a triangular saffron flag at the top. That's how you find the gurdwara. It's the Nishan Sahib, and every gurdwara flies one. But in Amritsar, at the Akal Takht, facing the Golden Temple, there are two, side by side. Look closely: they aren't quite the same height. Today: two flags at the Akal Takht.
screen: `A SAFFRON FLAG ABOVE THE ROOFTOPS.` → `EVERY GURDWARA HAS ONE.` → `AT THE AKAL TAKHT, TWO.`

segments.voice: Nishan means a sign, a mark; sahib is a word of honor. So the Nishan Sahib is the honored sign, the flag that says: here is a gurdwara, here you can find shelter and food. It carries the khanda, the Sikh emblem. Akal means timeless, beyond death: one of the oldest names Sikhs use for God. Takht means throne. Guru Hargobind raised the Akal Takht in 1606, the same years he took up the two swords, right across from the Harmandir. The Harmandir was the place of prayer; the Takht, where the community's worldly affairs were heard and decided. It's still the highest seat of Sikh authority. Between them stand the two Nishan Sahibs, called by the names of Guru Hargobind's swords. Miri is worldly sovereignty: responsibility for justice, for the community, for the world as it is. Piri is spiritual sovereignty: the Name, prayer, the life of the soul. And the piri flag stands slightly higher. That's the whole lesson, written in the sky. The Sikh tradition doesn't ask its people to pick between the world and the spirit. It raises both. But it doesn't pretend they're equal either. Worldly power is meant to answer to the spiritual; courage is meant to serve prayer, not the other way round. Two poles, a short walk apart, and the difference in height is small enough to miss. That's fitting too. The spirit doesn't have to tower. It just has to be a little higher.
screen: `NISHAN SAHIB — THE HONORED SIGN.` · `AKAL TAKHT — THE TIMELESS THRONE.` · `MIRI AND PIRI, SIDE BY SIDE.` · `THE PIRI FLAG STANDS SLIGHTLY HIGHER.` · then, large: `SPIRIT A LITTLE HIGHER.`

segments.voice: If you can, stand up, feet under your hips, and let your spine grow tall like a flagpole, the crown of your head lifting a little higher, breathing easily for a minute. Then sit, keep that little lift, and ask yourself: in my day, what's the higher flag?
Piri, spiritual sovereignty. The miri flag for worldly rule, the piri flag for the spirit, and the spiritual one a little higher.
Your line: spirit a little higher. Both flags fly; one just stands a bit taller. Day two hundred seventy-five, done.

276.title: Is that a knife?
276.hook: when someone asks about the kirpan, a calm short answer: an article of faith, kirpa and aan, mercy and honor
276.howItsDone: Initiated Sikhs wear the kirpan at all times as one of the five Ks, sheathed on a cloth strap called a gatra and often under the clothes; when asked, many explain it briefly as an article of faith, often read as kirpa and aan, mercy and honor, and check the local rules for airports, schools and work.

segments.voice: Yesterday, piri: two flags at the Akal Takht, and your line, spirit a little higher. Today, back to the small sword, and the question people ask about it most. Day two hundred seventy-six.

The airport security line. A school office on the first day of term. A new job, and a coworker who noticed a strap under a shirt. Three places, one question, sometimes asked kindly, sometimes not: is that a knife? A week ago you met the kirpan as a duty to protect. Today, what to actually say when someone asks.
screen: `AN AIRPORT. A SCHOOL. A NEW JOB.` → `IS THAT A KNIFE?` → `WHAT TO SAY.`

segments.voice: Start with an answer that fits in one breath. Something like: it's a kirpan, an article of my faith; it stands for protecting people who can't protect themselves, and it's never used in anger. Most people only need that much. If they want more, give them the name. Sikh teachers often explain kirpan as two words. Kirpa: grace, mercy, the word the Guru Granth Sahib uses again and again for God's kindness. And aan: honor, dignity. Language scholars trace kirpan to an older Sanskrit word for a blade, so mercy and honor is a teaching reading rather than the root. But notice the order. Mercy comes first. Then the practical part, said plainly. A kirpan is worn sheathed, on a cloth strap called a gatra, often small and under the clothes. Rules at airports, schools and workplaces differ from place to place. Airports in many countries allow no blade in the cabin, so Sikhs who fly plan ahead in different ways. Courts in some countries have accepted the kirpan as a religious article with safeguards, like a sheath sewn shut. If you carry one, your gurdwara or a Sikh civil-rights group can tell you what applies where you live. And if you don't carry one, the same short answer helps when someone asks you about a friend who does. Many Sikhs add one thing: how you answer is part of what the kirpan means. Calm, kind, unashamed. Mercy first.

segments.voice: Think of a question people ask about who you are, or about someone you love: your name, your clothes, your faith, your family, and picture someone asking it, a little nervous, a little blunt. Notice your first reaction, the tightening, breathe out through it, and find a calm answer in one sentence, in your own words, kind to them and true to you. Say it silently once, and picture them nodding.
The kirpan. An article of faith, often explained as kirpa and aan, mercy and honor, and best explained the same way: calmly, mercy first.
Your line: mercy first. In the answer, as much as in the sheath. Day two hundred seventy-six.

277.title: When the sword is right
277.hook: the Zafarnama says that when every other means has failed, it is right to take up the sword (Zafarnama 22)
277.howItsDone: Sikhs cite the Zafarnama, Guru Gobind Singh's Persian letter to Aurangzeb, for the principle that force is justified only as a last resort, after every other means has failed.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the kirpan, and one calm answer: kirpa and aan, mercy first. Today, the hardest question about any sword: when, if ever, is it right?

Winter. A city has been under siege for months. The men outside swore solemn oaths, on what they held holiest, that the people inside could leave in safety. The oaths broke the moment they stepped outside. In the weeks that followed, the man who led them lost all four of his sons. Almost everything, gone in a single winter. Then he sat down and wrote a letter to the emperor behind it all. Today: when the sword is right.
screen: `A CITY BESIEGED.` → `SOLEMN OATHS, BROKEN.` → `A LETTER TO THE EMPEROR.`

segments.voice: The man is Guru Gobind Singh. The winter is 1704 into 1705. After the siege of Anandpur and the broken oaths, his two elder sons died fighting at Chamkaur. His two youngest, still small boys, were executed at Sirhind. Tradition says the Guru wrote the letter soon after, in Persian verse, the language of the Mughal court, and sent it to the emperor Aurangzeb. It's called the Zafarnama, the letter of victory. A strange title after so much loss. But the victory it claims isn't on a battlefield. It's moral. The letter doesn't beg, and it doesn't rage. It calmly reminds the emperor of the oaths his men swore, and says a ruler who breaks his word has lost something no army can win back. And one couplet, number twenty-two in the usual numbering, sets out a principle. In plain words: when every other means has been tried and has failed, it is right to take hold of the sword. Notice where the weight falls. Not on the sword. On everything before it: talking, petition, patience, agreements. Every other means. The sword is not the first answer. It's the last one, and only when the others are truly used up. That's the line Sikhs point to when people ask how a tradition of prayer can carry a blade. Force isn't forbidden, but it has to earn its place by coming last. Most days, of course, the question never reaches the sword. It stops at the next conversation, the next try.
screen: `ANANDPUR, THEN CHAMKAUR AND SIRHIND.` · `ZAFARNAMA — THE LETTER OF VICTORY.` · `THE VICTORY IS MORAL, NOT MILITARY.` · `ONLY WHEN EVERY OTHER MEANS HAS FAILED.` · then, large: `EVERY OTHER MEANS FIRST.`

segments.voice: Think of a conflict in your life that's stuck, one you may have already decided to fight out, go cold on, or give up. Before you do, run through the other means: have you asked plainly, listened fully, put it in writing, asked someone to help, waited a day? Find one peaceful way you haven't really tried yet, and picture yourself trying it.
Zafarnama, the letter of victory. Its principle: the sword is right only when every other means has been tried and has failed.
Your line: every other means first. The sword, if ever, comes last. That's day two hundred seventy-seven.

278.title: Rules of a righteous fight
278.hook: tradition holds that a just fight never harms the unarmed, the fleeing or the innocent
278.howItsDone: Sikhs speak of dharam yudh, a righteous fight taken up only in defense of justice, and remember Bhai Ghanaiya, who gave water to the wounded of both sides, as its example; Sikh relief and first-aid groups today often point to his example.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Zafarnama: the sword only when every other means has failed. Today, the next question. If a fight does come, how must it be fought?

Even a fight between two kids in the back seat has rules. No hitting below the belt. Leave the little one out of it. When somebody says stop, you stop. Break those, and the fight turns into something uglier, and everyone in the car can feel it. Armies need rules like that too, and they haven't always kept them. The Sikh tradition has a name for a fight that keeps its rules: dharam yudh.
screen: `EVEN THE BACK SEAT HAS RULES.` → `BREAK THEM, AND IT TURNS UGLY.` → `A FIGHT THAT KEEPS ITS RULES.`

segments.voice: Dharam is duty, righteousness, the right order of things. Yudh is war, battle. Dharam yudh: a righteous fight. Not for land, loot or revenge, but taken up as a last resort, in defense of what is right. Sikh tradition holds that such a fight has limits. You don't strike the unarmed. You don't pursue someone who's running away. You don't harm those who surrender, or women and children, or anyone who isn't fighting. You don't plunder homes or desecrate places of worship. These rules come mostly from tradition and the old Sikh histories, not from one list in scripture, and historians will tell you not every battle lived up to them. But the ideal is clear, and Sikhs tell one story to show it. During the battles around Anandpur, a Sikh named Bhai Ghanaiya crossed the battlefield with a water skin, giving water to the wounded. All the wounded, including soldiers fighting against the Sikhs. Some Sikhs were furious, and brought him to Guru Gobind Singh. Why are you helping the enemy? Tradition says Bhai Ghanaiya answered that he saw no friend or enemy on that field. In every face he saw the Guru. The Guru didn't scold him. He gave him ointment, and told him to dress their wounds as well. Sikhs today often remember Bhai Ghanaiya as a forerunner of humanitarian aid. That's the heart of dharam yudh: even in the middle of a fight, the other person never stops being a person.
screen: `DHARAM — RIGHT. YUDH — FIGHT.` · `NEVER THE UNARMED, FLEEING OR INNOCENT.` · `BHAI GHANAIYA'S WATER SKIN.` · `THE ENEMY IS STILL A PERSON.` · then, large: `FAIR, EVEN IN CONFLICT.`

segments.voice: Think of a disagreement you're in right now, at work, at home or online, and picture the other person as a face, not a position. Check your own rules of the fight: am I fair to what they actually said, am I hitting where they can't defend, am I dragging in someone who isn't part of it? Pick one rule you'll keep, even if they don't.
Dharam yudh. A righteous fight: taken up only for what's right, and never against the unarmed, the fleeing or the innocent.
Your line: fair, even in conflict. Bhai Ghanaiya's water skin says it best. Day two hundred seventy-eight, done.

279.title: Gatka, the moving prayer
279.hook: the Sikh martial art, practiced with sticks and swords, often as a moving meditation
279.howItsDone: Gatka is taught in gurdwaras and Sikh youth groups; teams perform it at nagar kirtan processions and at Hola Mohalla in Anandpur, and practitioners often keep Waheguru in mind as they move.

segments.voice: Yesterday, dharam yudh: a fight with rules, where the enemy is still a person. Today, where those old skills live now: in a circle cleared on the street.

A Sikh procession on a festival day. The road is cleared in a wide circle. A drum starts. Two young people step into the space with wooden sticks and small round shields, and they begin to circle each other, feet light, sticks flashing, the crowd shouting. It looks like a fight. Then you notice their faces. Calm. Focused. Almost peaceful. And sometimes their lips are moving. Today: gatka, the moving prayer.
screen: `A CLEARED CIRCLE, A DRUM.` → `STICKS FLASHING, FEET LIGHT.` → `CALM FACES, MOVING LIPS.`

segments.voice: Gatka is the Sikh martial art. In its best-known form today, it's practiced with a wooden stick, the soti, and a small shield, the phari. Some practitioners also train with swords, spears and other traditional weapons. It grew out of older fighting arts the Sikhs of the Gurus' time trained in, when the Khalsa had to defend itself. Today gatka appears at nagar kirtans, the processions that carry the Guru Granth Sahib through the streets, and especially at Hola Mohalla in Anandpur, the spring festival of martial skill that tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh. There are gatka competitions and teams too, with rules, points and safety gear. But teachers often say scoring isn't the heart of it. Gatka rests on footwork, a pattern of steps called the paintra. You learn balance and rhythm before you ever swing a stick. And the movement, they say, should be done in remembrance: Waheguru in the breath, the Name kept in mind while the body moves. That's why people call it a moving prayer. It's the saint-soldier in one practice. The body trained, strong and quick. The mind still and remembering. And the point isn't to hurt anyone. It's to be ready, and steady, at the same time.
screen: `SOTI AND PHARI — STICK AND SHIELD.` · `NAGAR KIRTAN AND HOLA MOHALLA.` · `PAINTRA — FOOTWORK FIRST.` · `THE BODY MOVES, THE MIND REMEMBERS.` · then, large: `MOVE WITH PRAYER.`

segments.voice: If you're able, stand, and shift your weight slowly from one foot to the other, arms loose, as if you were holding a light stick. Keep the breath slow, and with each step give the mind one word to rest on: a word you pray with, if you pray, or simply now. After a minute, come to stillness and sit.
Gatka. The Sikh martial art of stick, shield and sword, often practiced as a moving meditation: the body quick, the mind remembering.
Your line: move with prayer. Footwork first, and the Name in the breath. See you tomorrow.

280.title: The Nihangs
280.hook: blue-robed Sikh orders who keep the old martial traditions alive
280.howItsDone: Nihang orders live communally in camps called chhaunis, wear blue with the tall dumalla turban, keep horses and traditional weapons, and gather in great numbers at Hola Mohalla in Anandpur each spring.

segments.voice: Yesterday, gatka: move with prayer, the body quick, the mind remembering. Today, the people who never stopped living the old martial ways.

Anandpur, in spring, at Hola Mohalla. Out of the dust come riders on horseback, standing in the stirrups at a gallop, spears raised. They wear deep blue robes. Their turbans are enormous, stacked high, ringed with small steel circles and emblems that flash in the sun. It looks like a scene from three hundred years ago, and in a way it is. These are the Nihangs. Today, i'll introduce them, then look back on a week of sword and saint.
screen: `ANANDPUR, IN SPRING.` → `RIDERS IN DEEP BLUE.` → `TURBANS RINGED WITH STEEL.`

segments.voice: The Nihangs are orders of Sikh warriors who keep the Khalsa's old martial life going. They're sometimes called Akali Nihangs, from Akal, the Timeless: the ones who belong to the Timeless. They wear blue, a color tradition links to Guru Gobind Singh. They tie the tall turban called a dumalla, often carrying small steel weapons and quoits, the chakkar, in its folds. They keep horses, train with traditional weapons, and many live a traveling, communal life in camps called chhaunis. In the eighteenth century, when the Khalsa was fighting to survive, Nihang bands were among its fiercest defenders. Where the name comes from, sources disagree. Some explain it from a Persian word for a crocodile, fearless in the water. Others from roots meaning without fear, or without attachment. Nobody can settle it, and each explanation says something Nihangs value. Not every Sikh lives like a Nihang; they're a small part of the panth. But at Hola Mohalla, the spring gathering tradition traces to Guru Gobind Singh at Anandpur, it's the Nihangs' riding and mock battles that much of the crowd comes to see. Now, the week. The saint-soldier: prayer and courage in one person. Piri, the spirit a little higher. The kirpan, mercy first. Zafarnama: every other means first. Dharam yudh: fair, even in conflict. Gatka: move with prayer. And the Nihangs: the old ways kept. Tomorrow, the last day of this stretch, and the fight the Gurus cared about most.
screen: `AKALI NIHANGS — THOSE OF THE TIMELESS.` · `BLUE ROBES, TALL DUMALLA, HORSES.` · `A NAME WITH MANY EXPLANATIONS.` · `A WEEK OF SWORD AND SAINT.` · then, large: `THE OLD WAYS KEPT.`

segments.voice: Think of someone who keeps an old way alive: a grandparent who cooks the family dish from memory, a neighbor who mends instead of throwing away, a friend who still writes letters by hand. Picture them doing it, and notice the patience in it, and what would be lost if nobody did. If you like, choose one old way of your own you'd like to keep going.
